question: arXiv:2610.26648v1 builds the systematic covariance matrix of its Galactic Center spectrum from control regions along the Galactic plane, as the earlier template analysis by Cholis, Zhong, McDermott and Surdutovich did, but it treats the principal components of that matrix differently. How many principal components does each analysis keep in the covariance matrix it fits with, and what reason does each give? What does each quote for the share of the first three components, and what does the earlier paper report about its fits when fewer components are kept?

arguments.query: Cholis Zhong McDermott Surdutovich Galactic Center excess template

first_line.asked: query='Cholis Zhong McDermott Surdutovich Galactic Center excess template'

arguments.answer: Kim, Kang & Shin (2610.26648v1) keep all 14 principal components. They fit with the full 14×14 empirical covariance matrix (numerical rank 14) plus a diagonal statistical term, with no PCA truncation. Their reason is that ~99% retained variance doesn't by itself show the discarded modes are noise or that truncation leaves the spectral-fit results unchanged. They quote PC1 = 94.2% of the total variance and the first three together = 98.95%, as diagnostics only. Cholis et al. (2112.09706v2) keep only the first 3 PCs. They do this to remove small eigenvalues likely due to noise, which makes inversion more robust and avoids counting noise from other regions as systematic error. They quote Σ(w_i, i=1..3) ≈ 0.99, so the truncated matrix represents the original with 99% accuracy (their text gives no separate figure for PC1; it only says PC1 dominates). They report that their GCE fits are robust when three or more PCs are included, but fit quality degrades substantially in all cases when two or fewer PCs are used.
